idiom_name: named methods plus cmp/slices generic helpers and self-referential constraints
implementation_notes: Go forbids operator overloading, so there is no operator family to donate: a type expresses behaviour through methods (Equal, Compare) and the shared comparison machinery works over ordered type parameters - cmp.Ordered includes built-in numeric and string types plus user-defined types whose underlying type is one of them, cmp.Compare/cmp.Less build orderings on those values, and slices.SortFunc/SortStableFunc take comparator functions. The structural analogue of the CRTP mixin is a self-referential generic constraint (type Comparer[T any] interface { Compare(T) int }, used as Comparer[E] so a generic container can require comparison without storing a function field); that is worth it for containers and algorithms, not for ordinary domain types.
alternative: Explicit named methods (Money.Equal, Money.Compare) plus generic helpers - cmp.Compare and slices.SortFunc for user-defined types, cmp.Ordered for built-in or named numeric/string types - and a self-referential Comparer[E] constraint where a generic container needs an ordering; Go offers user types no operator participation at all.
pitfalls: cmp.Ordered includes named numeric and string types but not structs, so a generic algorithm still cannot be reused for a Money struct without a separate constraint - a frequent surprise when porting operator-based C++ code.
Method sets are per type and not extensible: embedding a base struct only promotes methods, never operators, and there is no way to add an operator to a family at all.
Comparison semantics are convention, not compiler-checked: nothing enforces that Compare is consistent with Equal, so maps (which use ==) and sorts (which use Compare) can silently disagree.
